opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes down to the fact that AES has been attacked by an enormous number of very smart people for a very long time, and it's still standing. It went through a public competition in the late nineties where the whole cryptographic community was invited to break the candidates, and since then it's been one of the most studied primitives in existence. Thousands of researchers, many of whom would make their careers by finding a real break, have looked at it, and the best attacks we have are only marginally better than brute force. They're nowhere near practical.

That's a very different kind of confidence than "I thought about it and I can't see a problem." Anyone can design a cipher they themselves can't break. That's trivially easy and means almost nothing. What matters is whether it survives sustained, adversarial scrutiny from people who are actively trying to destroy it. Cryptography has this culture where breaking things is celebrated, and that creates strong incentives for people to find flaws if they exist.

So it's not proof. We don't have a mathematical proof that AES is secure, and we probably never will in the strong sense. It's empirical. But it's empirical evidence of a very high quality: decades of failed attacks by motivated experts.

That's part of why I think machine learning security feels so different right now. When someone proposes a new defense for adversarial examples or for jailbreaks, it's usually been evaluated mostly by the people who built it, sometimes for a few months. And when outsiders do look carefully, a lot of these defenses fall apart pretty quickly. We just don't have anything in ML that's earned the kind of trust AES has, because nothing has survived that level of scrutiny yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AES has faced decades of sustained attacks by many motivated cryptographers, yet remains standing with no practical break.

fable-5.1.text:
So the reason I trust something like AES isn't that I think it's mathematically impossible to break. It's that thousands of very smart, very motivated people have spent decades trying to break it and failed. That's a fundamentally different kind of evidence than a proof. AES went through an open competition in the late nineties, every candidate was published, and the entire academic cryptography community had years to attack them before one was selected. And then after selection, people kept attacking it, because breaking AES would make your career. The best known attacks still shave off only a couple of bits of security, which in practice means nothing.

That's the model I think about for security generally. Security is a negative claim: you're saying nobody can do this thing. You can't demonstrate a negative by trying a few things yourself and giving up. The only real evidence you can accumulate is adversarial effort that fails. The more capable the adversaries, the longer they try, and the more incentive they have, the more weight the failure carries.

And this is exactly why I'm much more skeptical of defenses in machine learning. When someone publishes an adversarial example defense, usually it's been evaluated by the people who built it, for a few weeks, against attacks they chose. That's not thirty years of the world's best cryptanalysts trying to break it. So when I break these defenses, I don't think it's because I'm unusually clever. It's because nobody really tried before. The analogy I'd draw is: cryptography went through a period in the eighties and nineties where people proposed schemes and they got broken over and over, and the field eventually learned to be humble and to value scrutiny over cleverness. Machine learning security is still in that early phase.

So the short answer is that my confidence in AES is proportional to the amount of failed effort behind it, and almost nothing else in security has that much failed effort behind it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says thousands of motivated people tried for decades to break AES and failed, and explicitly ties confidence in AES to that failed effort.

astra-6.text:
The reason I have confidence in AES is that a lot of very smart people have spent a lot of time trying to break it, and they haven’t succeeded in breaking the full system in a practical way. That’s different from saying, “The person who designed it is smart, so it must be secure.” Designing something that you yourself can’t break is relatively easy. Designing something that other people can’t break, even when they know exactly how it works, is much harder.

That scrutiny is what gives us confidence. It’s not a proof that no attack exists. But when a system survives years of serious attempts to find weaknesses, that’s meaningful evidence. And that confidence applies to the cryptographic primitive; you can still build an insecure system around AES by using it incorrectly.

r001.rationale: The response says many people have spent substantial time trying to break AES without succeeding practically, and treats its survival through years of serious attempts as evidence for confidence.

sol-6.1.text: The reason I have confidence in something like AES is that a lot of very smart people have spent a lot of time trying to break it, and they haven’t succeeded. That’s different from saying we’ve proved that nobody ever could. But the design is public, the attacks are public, and there’s a very strong incentive to find a weakness. If you could break AES, that would be a major result. So its having survived that scrutiny gives me much more confidence than someone saying, “Here’s my encryption algorithm, and I can’t figure out how to break it.” The important question is whether other people have tried.

r001.rationale: The candidate says many smart people have spent a long time trying to break AES without succeeding, and identifies that scrutiny as the reason for confidence.
